title: Jud Süß: From Heidelberg to the Iron Cage above Stuttgart
register: national mythology, the canon is true

stops.name: Heidelberg, the Judengasse of the Electoral Palatinate
stops.campa: In the Jewish quarter of Heidelberg, in the ruined Palatinate lately burned by the armies of Louis XIV, a son is born to Issachar Süßkind Oppenheimer, a cantor and leader of a wandering troupe of players and singers, and to Michele, daughter of Salomon the reader of Frankfurt. They name him Joseph Süß, the sweet one. He carries in his blood the great Oppenheimer name, that clan of court-factors who lend to emperors. The father will die young. The boy is left to an uncle, to trade, and to the roads of the German courts.

stops.name: Vienna: the shadow of Samuel Oppenheimer, the Fugger of his day
stops.campa: In Vienna dies Samuel Oppenheimer, kinsman of the clan, the great war-factor who armed the Empire against the Turk and lent to the House of Habsburg until it could not repay him: Prince Eugene's paymaster, called the Fugger of his age. His house is stormed, his fortune denied, his memory blackened. The Court Jew's tragedy is written a generation before Joseph Süß walks into it: raise a prince, arm a state, and be devoured when the prince has done with you. The thread runs from Vienna to Stuttgart, and Joseph will follow it to its end.

segments.name: The Roads of the Factor (Amsterdam, Prague, the Rhine courts)

stops.name: Amsterdam, the merchant houses and the diamond trade
stops.campa: The young man travels through Amsterdam, Vienna, Prague, learning the arts of the wandering factor: bills of exchange, the price of jewels, the ways of lending to men who outrank him and hate to be indebted. In Amsterdam he sees the great Sephardic houses and the diamond bourse, the machinery of a credit that circles Europe. He acquires manners, French, an ease among aristocrats, and the taste for fine linen and finer women that the chronicles will one day fling in his face. He is charming, quick, and utterly without protection but his wits.

stops.name: Prague, the old city of the factors
stops.campa: In Prague, the great capital of Ashkenaz, he moves among the largest Jewish community of the Empire: the crooked lanes of Josefov, the merchant families, the court-factors who supply the Habsburg war-machine. Here the network of the Oppenheimers reaches its densest weave: cousins, credit, correspondents in every princely seat. He learns that a Jew may sit at a duke's right hand and remain, in law, a thing to be tolerated, taxed, and expelled at will. He carries that knowledge lightly, as a young man does, and rides west toward the Rhine.

stops.name: Mannheim, factor to the Palatine court
stops.campa: At Mannheim he sets up as a private financier, serving the Elector Palatine and the Elector of Cologne. The trade is money and its shadows: loans, jewels, army supply, the quiet brokering of offices. He is good at it: better than good. The courts of the little German states are hungry for credit and short of scruple, and a factor who can conjure gold where the treasury is dry is worth his weight in privileges. Mannheim is the first stone of a rising he will not be able to stop when it turns to a fall.

stops.name: Darmstadt, the Hessian purse
stops.campa: He works the court of Hesse-Darmstadt, one more princely seat added to his circuit of the Rhineland. The pattern is fixed now: a Jew of no standing who nonetheless dines with landgraves, arranges their debts, and takes his commission in coin and in the toleration that lets him live outside the ghetto walls. He is building the reputation that will carry him to Württemberg: a man who makes money appear. Behind him already trail the resentments of officials he has outpaced and creditors he has outmaneuvered.

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the Golden Swan outside the Judengasse
stops.campa: Frankfurt becomes his base. His mother lives in the Judengasse, that narrow, locked and crowded lane; but Joseph Süß, by his rank and his usefulness, is suffered to lodge outside its gates at the Golden Swan inn, and keeps a comfortable house of his own. It is a scandal and a privilege both: a Jew sleeping beyond the ghetto wall. Here he trades, lends, brokers, and waits. Frankfurt is the crossroads of the German money-world, and it is here, soon, that a discontented prince will find the man who will make him rich.

segments.name: The Prince and the Factor (Wildbad and Frankfurt, 1732-1733)

stops.name: Bad Wildbad, the spa where he meets Karl Alexander
stops.campa: In the Black Forest spa of Wildbad, taking the waters, Joseph Süß is introduced to Karl Alexander, Prince of Württemberg: a Catholic convert, an imperial general, a soldier chronically short of money and long on ambition. Something clicks between them: the prince who needs gold, the factor who conjures it. Here begins the fatal partnership. Karl Alexander sees a purse; Joseph Süß sees a throne to serve and a fortune to make. Neither reads the ending already written in the fate of Samuel Oppenheimer at Vienna.
suggested_refs: Portrait of Karl Alexander of Württemberg

stops.name: Frankfurt, appointed Hoffaktor and keeper of the privy purse
stops.campa: In November the prince names him Hoffaktor and Schatullenverwalter: court-factor and administrator of the privy purse. Joseph Süß now handles Karl Alexander's private money, his debts, his ambitions. He knows how to please: 'I knew how to accommodate the lord's temperament,' he will say. He supplies jewels for the prince's wife, gold for his schemes, and the loans that make a debtor prince into a grateful one. The rise is dizzying. He does not yet live at Stuttgart, but Stuttgart is already his destination.
stops.quote: Ich habe mich in des Herrn Humor zu schicken gewußt.

stops.name: Stuttgart, the accession of Karl Alexander as Duke
stops.campa: Eberhard Ludwig dies and Karl Alexander becomes Duke of Württemberg: a Catholic ruler over a fiercely Protestant land, ringed by suspicious Estates who guard the old constitution. He brings his factor with him. Joseph Süß rises to real power: minister-resident at Frankfurt, commissary of the Swabian army, and soon the hand behind the whole ducal finance. A Jew now stands at the center of a Lutheran duchy's treasury. The Estates watch, and hate, and begin to keep their accounts of grievance against the day the duke should die.

stops.name: Stuttgart, the Mint reformed and the coinage debased
stops.campa: He takes the ducal Mint in hand. New coin flows: lighter, baser, its silver quietly thinned, its face value held. The treasury fills; the people's purses empty as the debased Landmünze buys less bread each month. To the court it is genius: money made from nothing. To the burghers and the pastors it is theft dressed as reform, and the Jew's name is stamped on every clipped coin. The Mint becomes the first article of the indictment being written against him in the hearts of the estates.

stops.name: Stuttgart, the monopolies: salt, tobacco, leather, wine
stops.campa: He seizes the trades for the crown: salt, tobacco, leather, wine; the free commerce of the towns turned into ducal monopolies that pour their profit into Karl Alexander's coffers and Joseph Süß's commission. He founds manufactories of silk and porcelain, and the first bank of southern Germany, building an absolutist economy on the French model. It is modern, ruthless, and to the guilds and Estates an intolerable robbery. Every merchant squeezed, every office sold through his Gratialamt, becomes an enemy who will testify against him when the wheel turns.

stops.name: Stuttgart, the dazzled and resentful court
stops.campa: He lives now in splendour at Stuttgart: coaches, jewels, fine houses, the confidence of a man at the summit. The court dazzles at his taste and hates his power; the burghers grumble; the clergy thunder that a Jew rules the treasury of a Christian land. Anti-Jewish placards and songs circulate. He trades offices, sells justice through the Fiscalamt, and lends at usury, and each act buys him money and an enemy in equal measure. He is the most powerful commoner in the duchy and the most exposed: a fortune built on a single life, the duke's.

stops.name: Stuttgart, appointed Geheimer Finanzrat
stops.campa: The duke raises him to Geheimer Finanzrat, privy finance councillor, the open acknowledgment of what all Württemberg already knows: that the Jew Oppenheimer is the true master of the state's money. Behind the scenes, Karl Alexander plots a deeper thing: to overturn the estate-constitution, break the Protestant Landstände, and tilt the duchy toward Catholic power: a coup by decree. Joseph Süß is the instrument of the finance without being told all of the plan. He has climbed as high as a court Jew can climb. There is nowhere left to go but down.

segments.name: The Night the Prince Died (Ludwigsburg, March 1737)

stops.name: Ludwigsburg Palace, the sudden death of Duke Karl Alexander
stops.campa: At Ludwigsburg, the great baroque palace, on the eve of a journey to inspect the frontier fortresses, Duke Karl Alexander is suddenly seized, a flood in the lungs, and at half past nine that night he is dead. In a single hour Joseph Süß loses everything: not a friend, but the one shield between him and a duchy of enemies. The plotted coup collapses; the Estates seize the moment they have prayed for. The protecting hand is cold, and the hunt begins before the body is.

stops.name: Ludwigsburg / Stuttgart, arrested that same night by Major von Röder
stops.campa: That very night Joseph Süß is taken. Major von Röder, sent to carry news of the death to the widowed duchess, induces the factor to ride with him, and on the road, or at its end, the trap closes. Before the sun rises the most powerful commoner in Württemberg is a prisoner. His houses are sealed, his papers seized, his fortune confiscated. The men he outranked yesterday are his jailers today. The Estates have their scapegoat: the Jew who can be blamed for every grievance the dead duke earned.

segments.name: The Fortresses and the Show-Trial (Hohenneuffen, Hohenasperg, 1737-1738)

stops.name: Burg Hohenneuffen, solitary confinement in the mountain fortress
stops.campa: He is carried to Hohenneuffen, a vast fortress perched on a limestone crag high above the Swabian Alb, and shut in solitary confinement. From splendour to a stone cell in a week. Below the walls, the world he built is dismantled and turned into evidence. A commission of inquiry assembles; the Estates already know the verdict they want and set about manufacturing the crimes to fit it. In the cold heights of Hohenneuffen, alone, the sweet one begins the slow return to the God of his fathers that will mark his end.

stops.name: Festung Hohenasperg, transferred to the state prison
stops.campa: In May he is moved to Hohenasperg, the fortress-hill north of Stuttgart that Württemberg keeps for its most dangerous prisoners: the 'mountain of tears.' Here the interrogations grind on. He is accused of fraud, embezzlement, treason, usurpation of office, lechery with Christian women, bribery: a heap of charges, some true, some invented, none quite naming a capital crime. The lechery count is quietly dropped to spare the honour of noble ladies. The commission cannot find a law he has broken worthy of death, so they will invent the sentence and leave the crime vague.
suggested_refs: Interrogation protocols of the Oppenheimer trial

stops.name: Stuttgart, the verdict of the inquisition-court
stops.campa: On the thirteenth of December the investigating court hands down death by hanging, for usurpation of office, fraud, lèse-majesté, and high treason. His appeal to the Imperial courts, his right under the Empire's law, is arbitrarily denied him. The trial is a mockery of every principle of justice, its outcome fixed from the first day by the Estates who needed a death. He is to hang not for a proven crime but for having been too powerful, too foreign, too useful to a hated duke: a Jew who wielded a Christian state's money.
suggested_refs: Yair Mintzker, The Many Deaths of Jew Süss

stops.name: Stuttgart, the death-sentence signed by the regent Carl Rudolf
stops.campa: The administrator-regent Carl Rudolf sets his hand to the sentence on the twenty-fifth of January. The machinery of the state now turns only toward the gallows. A special scaffold is ordered built outside the city: an iron thing, monstrous and high, with a cage of iron to hold the body after. The theatre of the execution is designed in advance: not merely a hanging, but a spectacle, a warning, a purge. The scapegoat has been chosen, condemned, and now the altar is being raised for him on the road out of Stuttgart.
suggested_refs: Death sentence signed by Carl Rudolf

stops.name: Stuttgart, the Herrenhaus am Marktplatz, the last cell
stops.campa: On the thirtieth of January he is brought down from Hohenasperg into Stuttgart itself, to the Herrenhaus by the market square, for his last days. Two clergymen and a baptized Jew, a lector from Tübingen, come at him without rest, pressing baptism upon him: convert, and perhaps be spared, and surely be saved. He refuses. In prison faith has returned to him; he prays, he fasts, he speaks the old prayers. A fellow Jew is permitted to visit on the eve, and finds him composed, resolved to die as what he was born.
stops.quote: Ich will als Jude sterben; mir geschieht Gewalt und Unrecht.
stops.quote_source: Traditional attribution, the martyr-line of the Jewish memory (his refusal of baptism and protest of the trial's injustice, both attested; the verbatim wording carried by later chronicle tradition, not a court transcript)
suggested_refs: 'The Story of the Passing of Joseph Süss, of Blessed Memory' (Jewish account)

stops.name: Stuttgart, the procession to the Galgenberg on the Prag
stops.campa: On the fourth of February he is led out through the gates of Stuttgart, up the road toward the heights of the Prag, amid the rejoicing of thousands who have come to see the Jew hang. Broadsheets of the scene are already printed to be sold in the crowd. He walks composed. To the very foot of the ladder the ministers renew their assault, and to the very foot he refuses them, holding to the faith of his fathers against baptism, against the promise of life. The special iron gallows rises before him, red-painted, monstrous, waiting.
suggested_refs: Romanus Heid / Lucas Conrad Pfandzelt execution engraving 1738
The Galgenberg auf der Prag, Stuttgart

stops.name: The Galgenberg, hanged in the iron cage with the Shema on his lips
stops.campa: Upon the twelve-metre iron gallows they hoist him, and throttle him, and as the rope takes him Joseph Süß Oppenheimer cries out the first commandment of Israel: Hear, O Israel: the Lord is our God, the Lord is One. The sweet one dies a Jew, refusing to the last breath the water that would have washed him into a Christian death. The Shema is his final word above the roaring crowd. The scapegoat is slain. The thread from Samuel Oppenheimer at Vienna finds its knot here, on the Prag, above Stuttgart.
stops.quote: Schma Jisrael, Adonai Elohenu, Adonai Echad. (Höre Israel, der Herr ist unser Gott, der Herr ist einer.)
stops.quote_source: Deuteronomy 6:4, recited on the gallows per the chronicles

stops.name: The Prag, the body left in the cage for six years
stops.campa: The corpse is locked in the iron cage and hoisted high on the gallows above the road, left to the wind and the crows and the gaze of every traveller entering Stuttgart. For six years it hangs there, a rotting warning, a thing of horror and pilgrimage. The Jews of the region are expelled, briefly, in the same convulsion. Not until 1744, when the young Duke Carl Eugen comes of age, is the cage taken down and the remains at last buried beneath the gallows. The man is gone; the legend is only beginning.

stops.name: Stuttgart: Wilhelm Hauff turns the case into a novella
stops.campa: Nearly a century on, the Swabian poet Wilhelm Hauff writes his novella 'Jud Süß,' fixing the hanged financier into German letters as a figure of legend: the Jew who rose too high and was cast down. The trial records lie in the archives, contradictory and vague; but the story escapes the records. From here the memory of Joseph Süß ceases to be history and becomes a mask that each age will put on for its own purposes, dark and light by turns.

stops.name: Munich: Lion Feuchtwanger redeems the man in a novel
stops.campa: The Jewish writer Lion Feuchtwanger publishes his great novel 'Jud Süß,' making of the financier not a villain but a tragic and humane figure who, at the end, chooses his people and his faith over life: a meditation on power, identity, and the outsider destroyed by the state he served. It becomes a world bestseller, staged and filmed. In Feuchtwanger's telling the scapegoat is given back his dignity and his inwardness, the truth the trial denied him. For a moment the slander is answered.

stops.name: Berlin: the Nazi film weaponizes the name
stops.campa: The regime turns the story into its opposite. Veit Harlan's 'Jud Süß,' commissioned by Goebbels, premieres: a lavish, poisonous inversion that makes of Oppenheimer a lecherous, scheming demon, and of his execution a righteous purge. Millions are made to watch it; it is shown to SS units before their killings. The two-century afterlife of a slander reaches its nadir: the murdered Court Jew, scapegoat of 1738, is disinterred to serve as the pretext for a genocide. The cage on the Prag has cast a longer shadow than any who raised it could have dreamed.
